docs.title: papers
docs.text:
Command-line tool to manage your bibliography (PDFs + BibTeX).

A light-weight, command-line bibliography management tool built like git, with a main command papers and a range of subcommands. It lets you:

  • Maintain a PDF library with appropriate, customisable file naming.
  • Maintain one or several BibTeX collections, linked to their PDFs.
  • Fetch metadata from the internet — enough PDF-parsing capability to pull metadata from crossref (by DOI or fulltext search) or google scholar.
  • Search and act on your library with a find/grep-inspired papers list (tag, edit, delete, rename, fetch, deduplicate).
  • Stay in control — plain BibTeX files, optional git tracking, and undo/redo for every change.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
pip install papers-cli
papers add mypaper.pdf --copy --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files
  • Installation — pip install and external dependencies.
  • Quickstart — extract metadata, add a PDF, list entries.
  • Adding entries — from PDFs, DOIs, bibtex, or whole directories.
  • Configuration — libraries, settings and pools.

Scientific writing & data

  • bard — text-to-speech reader.

docs.title: Adding entries
docs.text: The papers add command adds entries to your library, with or without a PDF attachment.

docs.title: Add a PDF (extract metadata automatically)
docs.text:
$> papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files --info
INFO:papers:found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:new entry: perrette_landerer2013
INFO:papers:mv /home/perrette/playground/papers/esd-4-11-2013.pdf files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf
INFO:papers:renamed file(s): 1

That is equivalent to doing:

papers extract esd-4-11-2013.pdf > entry.bib
papers add entry.bib --attach esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files

docs.title: What happens to the files
docs.text:
By default, papers add moves the PDF into the files directory of the library, under a name made from the name template. The files setting of the library changes that (see Files):

  • move (default): place the file in the files directory and remove the original;
  • copy: place it in the files directory and keep the original (a hard link when possible, otherwise a copy);
  • link: leave it where it is; the entry links to it there.

--move, --copy and --link override the setting for one command (-r/--rename is the same as --move, -c as --copy):

papers config files copy           # this library keeps the originals
papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --link

A file that belongs to another library (inside its files directory) is never moved: it is copied instead, so that the other library keeps its link.

The same applies to the files linked from the entries of a bibtex file added with papers add other.bib: their paths are read relative to that bibtex, and when they are linked where they are (link), they are stored so that they remain valid from your own bibtex (relative to it, or absolute, according to the paths setting of the library).

See Renaming files and keys for how to specify file naming patterns, and how the files of an entry with attachments are named.

docs.title: Attach files
docs.text: --attach FILE... attaches other files to the added entry (e.g. supplementary material), placed as the files setting says. They are named after the main file (see Renaming files and keys). To attach files to an entry already in the library, use papers file attach KEY FILE.... --attachment and -a are deprecated names of --attach.

docs.title: Add a whole directory of PDFs
docs.text:
It is possible to do this on a full directory of files, recursively, with -R/--recursive:

papers add -R /home/perette/playground/papers/papers_test

where, above, the papers_test directory contains a few PDF files. For each PDF, papers will attempt to extract the metadata and add the relevant file to the bibliography, and place the files as the files setting says (by default, moved into the files directory).

Files named after a PDF of the same directory, as papers names attachments (<name>--<label>.<ext> next to <name>.pdf, see Renaming files and keys), are added as attachments of that PDF's entry, whatever their type, instead of being scanned as papers of their own. Bibtex files found in the directory are added too, before the PDFs, and the files they link to are not scanned: their entry comes from the bibtex, so a folder that holds a bibtex and its files is added without looking anything up online. Folders of the pre-2.19 layout (with a hidden .<name>.bib) are read from their hidden bibtex.

The metadata of a PDF are found as follows:

  1. a DOI in the PDF metadata is used as is;
  2. otherwise, the DOIs printed in the text (first pages, and the last page, where some publishers add a cover page) are looked up in turn, and the first one whose title appears in the first pages is used: this skips the DOIs of cited papers;
  3. otherwise, a crossref search on the text of the first pages, whose result is also accepted only if its title appears in the text.

If none matches, the PDF is not added: pass its DOI with --doi (see below), or, for a reference without DOI (older papers, books, reports...), describe it and attach the PDF:

papers add --title "Self-consistent equilibrium ocean tides" --author "Agnew, Duncan C. and Farrell, W. E." \
    --year 1978 --journal "Geophysical Journal International" --attach agnew1978.pdf

docs.title: Entries already in the library
docs.text:
When the DOI of the added paper is already in the library (given with --doi, or found in the PDF metadata, or printed in the text of the PDF with the title of the library entry), papers add uses that entry: nothing is fetched online and there is no duplicate dialogue. The PDF (and the files of --attach) are attached to the entry and placed as the files setting says, as papers file attach KEY FILE... does; the key, the fields and the other files of the entry are not touched. An arXiv DOI (10.48550/arXiv.<id>) matches an entry whose eprint is that arXiv identifier. --no-check-duplicate skips this, and adds a new entry.

The order is: the library, then the pools (below), then online.

docs.title: Entries already in a pool
docs.text: Before querying crossref, papers add looks in the pools of the library (see Pools): a PDF with the same content as a pool file, or whose DOI is in a pool, a DOI that a pool entry has, or a bibtex entry that is the same paper as a pool entry, is taken from the pool, with its files. --no-pool skips this.

docs.title: Add an entry from its DOI
docs.text:
If you already know the DOI of a PDF, and don't want to gamble the fulltext search and match, you can indicate it via --doi:

papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013 --bibtex papers.bib

The add command above also works without any PDF (create a bibtex entry without file attachment):

papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013 --bibtex papers.bib

docs.title: Add an entry without DOI from bibtex + PDF
docs.text:
Some old files don't have a DOI. The best approach is to add the entry from its bibtex:

papers add entry.bib --attach esd-4-11-2013.pdf --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text: Before inserting an entry, papers add looks for the same paper in the library. papers check --duplicates and papers list --duplicates use the same rule (see Managing your library).

docs.title: Same paper
docs.text:
Two entries are the same paper when they have the same identifier, checked in this order:

  1. the DOI (case-insensitive; doi: and https://doi.org/ prefixes are ignored);
  2. the arXiv identifier: the eprint field when archivePrefix is arXiv or absent, and arXiv DOIs (10.48550/arXiv.<id>), whatever the version;
  3. the ISBN, for two @book entries only (a chapter carries the ISBN of its book, and each edition has its own ISBN);
  4. otherwise the family names of the authors and the title, compared without case, braces, accents and extra spaces. Both entries need authors and a title: two entries titled "Editorial" without authors are not the same paper.

The first identifier that both entries have decides: equal values make the same paper, different values two papers. A preprint and the published article with different DOIs are two entries, even with the same authors and title.

Equal identifiers make the same paper, except in one case: when the entry types differ (e.g. @book and @incollection) and the titles differ (after ignoring case, braces, accents and spacing), papers asks instead of merging. This happens with a chapter exported with the DOI of its book, or a dataset "Data for: X" deposited under the DOI of the article "X". Without a terminal, such a pair is never merged.

When you answer that two entries are not the same paper (n, below), papers records it in .papers/distinct.json, next to the bibtex, and does not ask about them again. The file records the identifiers of both entries (DOI, arXiv id, ISBN, authors and title), not their keys.

docs.title: What a merge does
docs.text:
The entry already in the library (entry 1) is the target:

  • it keeps its key;
  • fields that only the added entry has are added;
  • the file links of both entries are kept (a file linked twice, or two copies with the same content, once);
  • values that differ only by case, braces, spaces, or the case of a DOI are not conflicts, and the library's spelling is kept. Author names with initials and with full first names (Smith, J. and Smith, John) are not a conflict either: the fuller form is kept, whichever entry it comes from. Different first names (Smith, John and Smith, Jane) are a conflict;
  • the remaining differences are conflicts.

An added entry that brings nothing new (no conflict, no field to add) is merged without a question: its files are added, and papers prints already in library: smith2020climate (+1 file).

docs.title: --on-duplicate
docs.text:
--on-duplicate says what to do when the added entry has conflicts or fields to add:

Value What happens ask the dialogue below (default when the standard input is a terminal) keep merge; conflicts keep the library value update merge; conflicts take the value of the added entry skip the entry is not added; the library entry, its files and the added file are left as they are error stop before saving, and exit with status 1 (default without a terminal, e.g. in a script)

--no-check-duplicate adds the entries without looking for duplicates.

docs.title: The dialogue
docs.text:
$> papers add new.bib
Already in library: smith2020climate (same DOI 10.1000/abc123)
  1  library  smith2020climate  article  doi 10.1000/abc123  files/smith.pdf
  2  new      Smith_2020        article  doi 10.1000/ABC123  other/smith-preprint.pdf

@article{smith2020climate,
   author   = {Smith, John and Doe, Jane}
   doi      = {10.1000/abc123}
+  file     = {files/smith.pdf;other/smith-preprint.pdf}
!  journal  = {Nature}
!             2: {Nature Climate Change}
   keywords = {climate, mine}
   title    = {Climate sensitivity revisited}
+  volume   = {10}
   year     = {2020}
}
1 conflict. The key smith2020climate is kept; + lines are added.
  1 keep library values   2 take new values   f field by field   e edit
  n not the same paper (add Smith_2020 separately)   s skip   q quit   ? help
>>>

Unmarked lines are the same in both entries (here the title and the author names, which differ only by case and initials), + lines are added from the other entry, and ! lines are conflicts: the value that will be used, then the other values, numbered by entry.

Answer Meaning 1, 2 resolve all conflicts with the values of that entry, and merge f go through the conflicts one at a time e edit the merged entry in the editor, as plain bibtex; the values of the other entry are % comment lines below it. If the editor fails or the text is not one bibtex entry, papers comes back to this menu n not the same paper: add the entry separately (with a free key if its key is taken), and remember it s skip: change nothing for this entry; it is asked again next time q quit: skip this entry and all the remaining duplicates of this command; the other entries are added ? help

f asks for each conflict:

journal:
  1  Nature                 library
  2  Nature Climate Change  new
  [1/2/e] >>>

To stop without saving anything, use Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text: Entries added from a bibtex file keep their own key, unless -u/--update-key is passed, in which case the key is regenerated from the key template (see Renaming files and keys). Entries extracted from a PDF or fetched from a DOI always get a generated key. Either way, this only concerns entries new to the library: an entry merged into a duplicate takes the key of the library entry.

docs.title: Options of earlier versions
docs.text:
These options still work, with a warning, and will be removed:

Old New -m i --on-duplicate ask -m u --on-duplicate keep -m U --on-duplicate update (the library key is kept) -m o --on-duplicate update (the library key and the fields only in the library are kept) -m s --on-duplicate skip (the file of the added entry is not attached; keep does that) -m r --on-duplicate error -m a --no-check-duplicate --no-merge-files ignored: file links are always merged

docs.title: Why not JabRef, Zotero or Mendeley (or...) ?
docs.text:
• JabRef (2.10) is nice, light-weight, but is not so good at managing PDFs.
  • Zotero (5.0) features excellent PDF import capability, but it needs to be done manually one by one and is a little slow. Not very flexible.
  • Mendeley (1.17) is perfect at automatically extracting metadata from downloaded PDFs and managing your PDF library, but it is not open source, and many issues remain (own experience, Ubuntu 14.04, Desktop Version 1.17):
    • very unstable
    • PDF automatic naming is too verbose, and sometimes the behaviour is unexpected (some PDFs remain in an obscure Downloaded folder, instead of in the main collection)
    • somewhat heavy (it offers functions of online syncing, etc)
    • poor search capability (related to the point above)

Above-mentioned issues will with no doubt be improved in future releases, but they are a starting point for this project. Anyway, a command-line tool is per se a good idea for faster development, as noted here, but so far I could only find zotero clients for their online API (like pyzotero or zotero-cli). Please contact me if you know another interesting project.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
A library is a bibtex file, a files directory, and a configuration file next to them (.papersconfig.json). papers init creates one in the current directory, and papers init DIR in the directory DIR (created if missing, with its parents):

$> papers init
papers library: /home/perrette/projects/sealevel
version 3.0.0
* configuration file: .papersconfig.json
* global config:      /home/perrette/.config/papers/config.json (none)
* cache directory:    /home/perrette/.cache/papers
* backup (git):       True
* backup files (git-lfs): False
* backup directory:   /home/perrette/.local/share/papers/backups/sealevel-papers-3f9a1c2b
* files directory:    files (empty)
* bibtex:             papers.bib (empty)
* pools:
    default: /home/perrette/Documents/papers (missing)
...

By default the bibtex is papers.bib (or the first .bib file present in the directory) and the files directory is files (or an existing pdfs, pdf, papers or bibliography folder). The options of papers init are --bibtex, --filesdir, --pool NAME|PATH... (see Pools), --paths relative|absolute, --git/--no-git, --git-lfs, --editor, --light (see Light libraries) and the name and key format options (see Renaming files and keys). With DIR, the paths given to --bibtex and --filesdir are relative to DIR. papers init does not prompt, and fails if the directory already has a library configuration: change the settings of an existing library with papers config.

Every command run in the library directory or in one of its subdirectories acts on that library. -C DIR, before the command name, runs papers as if it was started in DIR:

papers -C ~/projects/sealevel list smith

--bibtex and --filesdir still override the library for one command. If the bibtex given with --bibtex belongs to another library (a configuration file in its directory or above), the settings of that library apply.

Outside of any library, commands act on the default pool if it is a library (see Pools), and otherwise fail with a message that explains how to create one.

Type papers status to see which library a command acts on, and papers status -v to also see its settings and where each one comes from.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
papers config gets and sets the settings, in the style of git config:

papers config                          # list the settings and where each comes from
papers config name.template            # print one setting
papers config name.template '{author}_{year}_{title}'   # set it in the library
papers config --unset name.template    # remove it from the library
papers config pools default ../shared  # settings with several values

Each setting comes from the library configuration if it sets it, otherwise from the global configuration, otherwise from its built-in default. papers config without argument shows the source of each setting as (library), (global) or (default).

Setting Values bibtex path of the bibtex file filesdir path of the files directory pools names or paths of the library's pools (default: default) paths relative (default) or absolute: how file links are written in the bibtex files move (default), copy or link: what papers add does with a file (see Files) sync none (default) or push: papers add also adds the new entries to the first pool (see Pools) git true or false: back up the bibtex with git (see Git integration) git-lfs true or false: also back up the files with git-lfs editor command that opens a text editor, e.g. vim or subl -w (it wins over $VISUAL and $EDITOR, which are used without it) name.template, name.author-num, name.author-sep, name.title-word-num, name.title-word-size, name.title-length, name.title-sep, name.unknown-template, name.unknown-strict file name format key.template, key.author-num, key.author-sep, key.title-word-num, key.title-word-size, key.title-length, key.title-sep, key.unknown-template, key.unknown-strict bibtex key format

The name and key settings correspond to the --name-* and --key-* options of the commands (see Renaming files and keys), which override them for one command.

Paths in the library configuration are stored relative to its directory, so that the library can be moved or shared as a whole. papers config bibtex, papers config filesdir and the list of papers config show them as absolute paths. A relative path given to set them is relative to the current directory.

Setting git to true initializes the backup directory and records the current bibtex. Setting paths rewrites the file links of the bibtex. light is not a setting of papers config: it is changed with papers migrate --light and papers migrate --full, because it also changes the file links and the files (see Light libraries).

docs.title: Global configuration
docs.text:
papers config --global reads and writes the global configuration (per user, as in git config --global) instead of the library's: ~/.config/papers/config.json on Linux (the platform's user configuration directory elsewhere). It holds the pool names and the default settings of the libraries that do not set them (everything except bibtex, filesdir and pools). It defines no library: the global library of papers v2 is now the default pool (see Pools).

papers config --global editor vim
papers config --global name.template '{author}_{year}'
papers config --global pools.teaching /mnt/shared/teaching
papers config --global                # list it

papers init stores paths, git and git-lfs in the new library, taking their values from the global configuration when it sets them. The other settings are only stored in the library when you set them.

docs.title: Pools
docs.text:
A pool is a library that other libraries exchange entries with (see Pools for add, pull, push, export and light libraries). Each library lists its pools in the pools setting, as names or paths. A name is looked up in the global configuration (pools.NAME, or papers pool add NAME PATH), so that the same library works on machines where the pool is in a different place. An entry that contains a / or starts with . or ~ is a path, relative to the library (e.g. ../shared-with-bob).

Without global configuration, the pool default is ~/Documents/papers. It is also the library that commands act on outside of any library, once it is one:

papers init ~/Documents/papers

papers status lists the pools of the library with their paths, says when a pool is missing or is not a library, and whether it changed since the last papers pull. It also shows whether the library is light, and the sync setting.

docs.title: Relative versus absolute paths
docs.text:
The file links in the bibtex are relative to the bibtex directory by default, so that a library folder can be moved or shared with its files. Set papers config paths absolute to store absolute paths instead, e.g. for a bibtex that links to files in a central folder.

The options --relative-paths and --absolute-paths of the commands still override the setting for one command, with a deprecation warning.

docs.title: Migrating from papers 2
docs.text:
papers migrate performs the one-time upgrades from version 2:

  • The global configuration of version 2 (~/.config/papersconfig.json on Linux) defined a library for the whole user account. papers migrate writes its settings to a library configuration next to its bibtex (if there is none yet), registers the directory of that bibtex as the default pool in the global configuration (unless another default pool is set there), and renames the old file to papersconfig.json.v2.bak. The bibtex, files and backup stay where they are. File links stay absolute, as they were, unless --relative is passed. Running papers migrate again does nothing. Until then, papers prints a warning and keeps using the global configuration outside of libraries.
  • papers migrate --folders moves the files of entries that are still kept in folders of papers before 2.19 (<name>/ with a hidden .<name>.bib) into the files directory, named after the name template (as papers file rename names them).

Library configurations (.papersconfig.json) of version 2 keep working without migration. The configuration files written by version 3 carry "version": 3; a file without version is read as a file of version 2. A file with a higher version was written by a newer papers, and papers stops with an error.

docs.title: papers install
docs.text: papers install is a deprecated alias of papers init that asks for the bibtex, the files directory and git (-y/--yes accepts the defaults; --no-prompt and --force are its deprecated forms). On an existing library it updates the library configuration, as in version 2, with a deprecation warning: use papers config instead (--edit and --reset keep working). papers install --global writes the library configuration next to the bibtex and registers its directory as the default pool; if a global configuration of version 2 exists, it first migrates it as papers migrate does. --local is ignored.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
papers uninstall

removes the library configuration and reports what it leaves behind (the bibtex file, the files directory, and the backup directory if any). Pass --remove-backup to also remove the backup directory. It never removes the global configuration. From outside of any library it does not remove the default pool's configuration: run papers -C DIR uninstall for that.

papers uninstall --recursive is deprecated and ignored (there is no global library configuration to walk up to in v3): only the configuration of the library is removed.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text: All internet requests, such as crossref requests, are saved in the cache directory (shown by papers status -v), whether or not a library is configured. The metadata of each DOI is a json file under doi/, e.g. doi/10.1126/science.1166510.json (DOIs that do not exist are remembered for a day). Deleting the directory, or any file in it, is safe: the requests are made again when needed.

docs.title: Current features
docs.text:
• parse PDF to extract DOI
  • fetch bibtex entry from DOI (using crossref API, or doi.org for DOIs registered elsewhere, e.g. DataCite)
  • fetch bibtex entry by fulltext search (using crossref API or google scholar)
  • create and maintain bibtex file
  • add entry as PDF (papers add ...)
  • add entry as bibtex (papers add ...)
  • scan directory for PDFs (papers add ...)
  • move, copy or link the added PDFs into a files directory (files setting, papers add --move/--copy/--link)
  • rename PDFs according to bibtex key and year (papers file rename [--keep-source])
  • move files and folders and update the links (papers file mv)
  • attachments (e.g. supplementary material), named after the main file (papers add ... --attach FILE, papers file attach KEY FILE)
  • duplicate detection by DOI, arXiv id, ISBN or authors and title, and merging (papers add, papers check --duplicates)
  • fix entries (papers check --format-name --encoding unicode --fix-doi --fix-key ...)
  • library configuration with its bibtex, files directory and settings (papers init --bibtex BIB --filesdir DIR ..., papers config)
  • integration with git
  • undo/redo command (papers undo / redo)
  • display / search / list entries: format as bibtex or key or whatever (papers list ... --format line|bibtex|key, or -l, --plain, -K)
  • edit, remove and tag entries by key or DOI, or from a pipe (papers edit, papers rm, papers tag, papers list ... -K | papers rm -)
  • check and fix file links (papers file check [--fix], papers file detach --broken, papers file clean):
    • report broken links, files linked twice and identical files
    • remove duplicate links (--fix)
    • fix files name after a Mendeley export (--fix):
      • leading / missing is added
      • latex characters, e.g. {\_} or {\'{e}} replaced with unicode

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Test coverage is improving (now 80%).

Currently covers:

  • papers extract (test on a handful of PDFs)
    • parse pdf DOI
    • fetch bibtex on crossref based on DOI
    • fetch bibtex on crossref based on fulltext search
    • fetch bibtex on google-scholar based on fulltext search
  • papers add
    • add entry and manage conflict
    • add pdf file, bibtex, directory
    • add one pdf file with attachments
    • conflict resolution
  • papers init, papers config, papers migrate, papers install
  • internals:
    • duplicate rule (identifiers and their order, title guard, .papers/distinct.json), merge and dialogue
  • papers list
  • papers undo / redo (partial)
  • papers file subcommands, papers rm, papers tag, papers edit
  • papers check --duplicates and the other checks (fix DOI etc.) (superficial)

docs.title: Files
docs.text: An entry links to its files (the PDF, supplementary material...) in its file field. The files usually live in the files directory of the library (the filesdir setting), named after the name template (see Renaming files and keys), but an entry can link to a file anywhere.

docs.title: What add does with a file
docs.text:
The files setting says what papers add does with the PDF it adds, with the files of the entries of an added bibtex (papers add other.bib), with the files of an added folder (papers add --recursive DIR) and with the files attached with --attach:

files the file is placed in the files directory the original is removed move (default) yes, under its template name yes copy yes, as a hard link when possible (same file system), otherwise a copy no link no: the entry links to the file where it is no

Set it for a library with papers config files copy, or for all libraries of the user with papers config --global files copy. The options --move, --copy and --link of papers add override it for one command; -r/--rename is the same as --move, and -c the same as --copy.

A file that belongs to another library, i.e. a file inside the files directory of a library whose configuration (.papersconfig.json) is found in the file's directory or above, is never moved: in move mode it is copied instead (a hard link when possible), so that the other library keeps its link. The same holds for a file in the files directory of a pool of the library (see Pools). A file already in the files directory of the current library is renamed in copy mode too, rather than copied next to itself. A file downloaded by papers (a URL given to add or --attach) is always moved into the files directory.

docs.title: papers file
docs.text:
The commands of papers file act on the files of the entries. Those that take entries accept keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs (see Naming entries), and - to read them from the standard input, one per line:

Command Action papers file rename [KEY...] place the files of the entries (all without KEY) in the files directory, under their template name; --keep-source keeps the originals too (hard links when possible) papers file mv SRC... DEST move files or folders, and update the links of the entries (below) papers file attach KEY FILE... attach files to an existing entry, following the files setting (--move, --copy, --link override it); the files the entry already has are not touched papers file detach FILE... [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files from every entry that links to them (only from the entries of --key with --key); the files are kept (below) papers file detach --key KEY... remove all the links of the entries papers file detach --broken [--key KEY...] remove the broken links (of all entries without --key) papers file rm FILE... [-r] [--key KEY...] remove the links to the files, then delete the files, like git rm (below) papers file check [KEY...] report broken links, files linked twice, identical files (same checksum) of an entry, and with --metadata a DOI of the PDF that differs from the DOI of the entry (this parses the PDFs) papers file clean remove the files of the files directory and its subfolders that no entry links to, asking for each one (-y/--yes does not ask)

papers file attach KEY FILE... is the low-level form of papers add FILE --doi DOI for an entry already in the library: when the DOI is that of a library entry, add attaches the file to it in the same way, without fetching anything (see Adding entries).

papers file check changes nothing unless --fix is passed. --fix only applies the repairs that cannot lose anything: paths saved by Mendeley (missing leading /, latex symbols such as {\_}) are repaired when the repaired path exists, and the second link to the same file, or to an identical file, is removed from the entry (the file itself stays on disk; papers file clean removes it). A broken link to a file of a pool (the pool renamed the file) is replaced by the pool entry's current file. Other broken links are reported, and removed with papers file detach --broken.

papers file clean skips hidden files and folders (such as .git) and .bib files. A folder of the layout of versions before 2.19 (with a hidden .<name>.bib) is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files.

docs.title: Moving files
docs.text:
papers file mv works like mv, with the rules of git mv, and updates the links of every entry that links to a moved file (links are compared by real path, so a link through a symbolic link is found too):

  1. a source file that no entry links to is an error;
  2. a source folder must contain at least one linked file; the whole folder moves, files that no entry links to included;
  3. with several sources, the destination must be an existing folder;
  4. a destination that exists as a file is an error, unless -f/--force (papers warns when entries link to the replaced file: their links then lead to the moved file);
  5. -n/--dry-run shows the moves and the links that change, and does nothing;
  6. moving the files directory of the library (or a folder that contains it) also updates the filesdir setting.

All checks run before anything moves: if one fails, nothing is moved. If a move fails midway (e.g. disk full), the bibtex is saved with the links of the files already moved, and the error is reported. The parent folders of the destination are created when needed. A folder that contains the bibtex or the library configuration cannot be moved with papers file mv.

papers file mv files/2013 files/archive/2013
papers file mv files ~/Documents/library-files    # also sets filesdir
papers file mv -n files/a.pdf files/b.pdf files/new/

Links from other libraries to the moved files break: papers cannot know about them.

docs.title: Detaching and removing files
docs.text:
A file can be linked from several entries: the chapters of a book that share the PDF of the volume, two papers that share a supplement. papers file detach FILE... removes the links to FILE from all of them and prints which entries lost a link. Links are compared by real path, so a broken link can be named too. The files stay on disk: papers file detach never deletes a file.

papers file rm FILE... works like git rm: it removes the links to FILE from every entry that links to it, then deletes the file.

  • A FILE that no entry links to is an error, and nothing changes (with --key: that none of the entries of --key links to).
  • -r FOLDER removes the linked files inside FOLDER (and its subfolders). Files that no entry links to stay where they are; the folders left empty are removed, FOLDER included, except the files directory of the library. Without -r, a folder is an error. papers file detach -r FOLDER removes the links in the same way, without deleting anything.
  • With --key, only the links of those entries are removed; a file that another entry still links to is kept on disk, and papers says so.
  • A file of a pool is never deleted (e.g. the files a light library links to): only the link is removed, and papers says so.
  • papers does not ask: the file was named on the command line. --dry-run shows the links that would be removed and the files and folders that would be deleted.

-k/--key takes one or more entries (keys, DOIs, arXiv identifiers or ISBNs), and can be repeated: --key K1 K2 is --key K1 --key K2; - reads them from the standard input. As it takes several values, write the files before it: in papers file rm --key K1 file.pdf, file.pdf would be read as an entry, and papers stops with the error file.pdf is not an entry: put the files before --key.

papers file detach files/volume.pdf                    # from all the chapters
papers file detach files/volume.pdf --key smith2020    # from one chapter
papers file detach --key smith2020                     # all its links
papers file rm files/old-version.pdf
papers file rm -r files/2013 --dry-run
papers list --tag draft -K | papers file detach --broken --key -

docs.title: Removing entries and their files
docs.text:
papers rm KEY... (or papers list ... --delete) removes entries. Their files that no remaining entry links to may be deleted too:

  • in a terminal, papers lists those that are inside the files directory and asks once whether to delete them (default: no);
  • --delete-files deletes them without asking, and also those outside the files directory; --keep-files keeps them without asking;
  • without a terminal (e.g. the keys come from a pipe), the files are kept, and papers lists them: papers file clean deletes them later;
  • a file outside the files directory is deleted only with --delete-files.

A file still linked from another entry is never deleted, nor a file in the files directory of a pool of the library (e.g. the files a light library links to, see Light libraries). A file that is a hard link (e.g. to the file of another library) can be deleted: this only removes this link, and papers says so.

docs.title: Deprecated forms
docs.text: papers filecheck still works in v3, with a warning, and runs the corresponding commands: --rename (-c) is papers file rename (--keep-source), --delete-broken is papers file detach --broken, --hash-check and --fix-mendeley are papers file check --fix, --metadata-check is papers file check --metadata, and --clean-filesdir (--force) is papers file clean (--yes). The file actions of papers list are deprecated too (see Listing and searching), and so is papers add --attachment (now --attach).

docs.title: Git-tracked library
docs.text:
By default (when a git binary is available), a library created with papers init git-tracks any change to the bibtex file. Pass --no-git to opt out, and --git-lfs to also back up the attached files (see below):

$> papers init --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files [ --no-git | --git-lfs ]

Libraries made by older papers versions keep their saved setting; run papers config git true (or papers config git-lfs true) to enable git-tracking on an existing library.

From now on, every change to the library will result in an automatic git commit. And the papers git ... command will work just as git ... executed from the backup directory. E.g. papers git remote add origin *REMOTE URL*; papers git lfs track files; papers git add files; papers git push. When git fails, it prints its own error message, and papers exits with git's exit code.

Under the hood, every save commits a copy of the bibtex file to the backup repository, with the files .papers/origin.bib (origin copies of the entries taken from pools, see Pools) and .papers/distinct.json (pairs that are not the same paper) when they exist. If --git-lfs is passed, the attached files are backed up along with the bibtex: they are hard-linked into the backup directory and tracked with git-lfs, together with a copy of the bibtex whose file paths point into the backup (so the backup is self-contained). Background in issue 51.

Backup occurs in a subfolder of ~/.local/share/papers/backups, whatever the location of the library. Type papers status -v to find out, or papers backup list to see every backup directory papers knows of and which library each belongs to. Orphaned directories (e.g. whose library was deleted) can be cleaned up with papers backup remove NAME (glob patterns allowed; asks before deleting unless -y/--yes is passed; -f/--force is the deprecated form).

Backup directories are named after the bibtex file and its parent folder, plus a hash of the full path (e.g. myproject-references-3f9a1c2b), so two libraries can never share a directory and same-named libraries remain recognizable. The library configuration stores the name of its backup directory, which each machine looks up in its own backup folder; only a backup directory outside that folder is stored as an absolute path. Each directory also contains a manifest.json recording the bibtex file it backs up; if a backup operation finds a directory that belongs to another library (which could happen with directories created by papers versions that used the bibtex name alone), it moves the current library to a fresh directory instead of mixing the two histories. Directories created by older versions keep their name and are adopted as-is.

For libraries that are already in a git repository, the feature remains useful as it is the basis for papers undo and papers redo (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Install papers
docs.text:
pip install papers-cli

Note there is another project registered on PyPI as papers, hence papers-cli for command-line-interface. The installed command is still papers.

docs.title: Name clash with GNOME Papers
docs.text:
The GNOME Papers document viewer (the default viewer on recent GNOME desktops) also installs a papers command; with both installed, whichever comes first in $PATH wins. Two mitigations are built in:

  • The package also installs the command under the unambiguous name papers-cli — call that, or set a shell alias (e.g. alias papers=papers-cli), on systems where the names collide.
  • Because this command may mask GNOME Papers, a call whose arguments are all existing files (paths or file:// URIs, as passed by file managers through the viewer's desktop entry) is handed over unchanged to the next papers executable in $PATH that is not this tool, i.e. GNOME Papers itself. Double-clicking a PDF and papers somefile.pdf therefore keep opening the viewer. If no other papers is found, the files are opened with the system's default viewer (xdg-open) instead; should that lead back to this command, it stops with an error rather than looping. Subcommand names always take precedence (papers ./list opens a file named list; papers list lists your library), and any flag disables the hand-over — call the viewer's binary directly for viewer-specific flags.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• python 3.11+
  • PyMuPDF (preferred) or poppler-utils (only pdftotext and pdfinfo; deprecated): convert PDF to text for parsing
  • bibtexparser: parse bibtex files
  • scholarly: interface for google scholar
  • rapidfuzz: calculate score to sort crossref requests
  • unidecode: replace unicode with ascii equivalent

The Python dependencies are installed automatically with pip.

docs.title: Move library to a new location
docs.text:
Moving a library can be tricky. Simple cases are:

  • files are stored in a central repository, and the bibtex contains absolute paths. Then moving the bibtex by hand is fine.
  • files are stored alongside the bibtex, and the bibtex contains relative paths. Just move around the folder containing bibtex and files.

In any other cases, you risk breaking the file links.

Papers tries to be as little opinionated as possible about how files are organized, and so it relies on your own judgement and use case. When loading a bibtex, it always interprets relative file links as being relative to the bibtex file. When saving a bibtex, it will save file links according to the paths setting of the library (relative to the bibtex by default, see Configuration).

To move the files directory, or some of its files, use papers file mv: it updates the links of the entries, and the filesdir setting when the files directory itself moves (see Files):

papers file mv files ../shared/files

The following set of commands also works, provided the initial file links are valid (optional parameters in brackets):

touch new.bib
papers add /path/to/old.bib --bib new.bib [ --copy | --link ] [ --filesdir newfilesdir ]
rm -f /path/to/old.bib

By default the files of old.bib are moved into the files directory (--copy keeps them in place too, --link links to them where they are), except the files inside the files directory of another library, which are copied.

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
It's easy to end up with duplicates in your bibtex. After adding PDFs, or every once in a while, do:

papers check --duplicates

It groups the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (same DOI, arXiv id, ISBN of two books, or else same authors and title; see Adding entries), and merges each group into one entry. A group never holds two entries with different DOIs: a copy without DOI that matches both goes with one of them, and the other comes up on the next check if it is still a match.

Entry 1 of a group, the target, is the entry with most fields. The merge works as in papers add: the target keeps its key, fields missing in it are added, the file links are kept. The other entries are removed, and their keys are added to the biblatex ids field of the target, so that \cite commands with the old keys keep working with biblatex (BibTeX ignores the field). Commands that take a KEY also accept a key of the ids field.

$> papers check --duplicates
Same paper: 2 entries (same title and authors)
  1  smith2020climate  article  doi 10.1000/abc123  files/smith.pdf
  2  Smith_2020        article  no doi              other/smith-preprint.pdf

@article{smith2020climate,
!  key      = smith2020climate
!             2: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)
   author   = {Smith, John and Doe, Jane}
   doi      = {10.1000/abc123}
+  file     = {files/smith.pdf;other/smith-preprint.pdf}
+  ids      = {Smith_2020}
!  journal  = {Nature}
!             2: {Nature Climate Change}
   keywords = {climate, mine}
   title    = {Climate sensitivity revisited}
   year     = {2020}
}
1 conflict. Entry 2 is removed after the merge; its key goes to ids.
  1 keep values of 1   2 take values of 2   f field by field   e edit
  t N make entry N the target   n not the same paper   s skip   q quit   ? help
>>> 1
merged into smith2020climate: Smith_2020 (kept in ids)

The answers are those of the dialogue of papers add (see Adding entries), with one more: t N makes entry N the target, so that its key is kept. n (not the same paper) leaves the entries as they are and records them in .papers/distinct.json, so that the next check does not ask again. A group whose entries differ only by key and file links is merged without a question.

--on-duplicate sets what to do with each group without asking:

Value What happens ask the dialogue (default when the standard input is a terminal) keep merge; conflicts keep the value of entry 1 skip leave the groups as they are (the default with -y/--yes) error exit with status 1 if there is any group, and list them (default without a terminal)

Groups that the title guard asks about (same DOI, but different entry types and titles) are never merged with keep.

To only see the groups, use papers list --duplicates (see Listing).

The -m/--mode option of earlier versions still works, with a warning: -m i is --on-duplicate ask, -m m is keep, -m s is skip. To remove entries, use papers rm.

docs.title: Checking and fixing files
docs.text:
papers file check reports broken links, files linked twice, identical files and, with --metadata, DOIs of PDFs that differ from their entry's DOI. It changes nothing unless --fix is passed, which applies the safe repairs only. Broken links are removed with papers file detach --broken:

papers file check
papers file check --fix
papers file detach --broken

papers file rename places the files in the files directory under their template name (see Renaming files and keys).

papers file clean removes the files of the files directory (and its subfolders) that no entry links to:

papers file clean

It asks before removing anything, unless -y/--yes is passed. It ignores hidden files and folders and .bib files; a folder with a .{folder}.bib file inside, which is how versions before 2.19 stored entries with several files (see Renaming files and keys), is removed as a whole when no entry links to its files. That command works best when the files are in their own folder, and not mixed up with other things, obviously.

papers file clean --dry-run --yes lists the files that no entry links to, without removing them: a way to check what is actually tracked and what is not.

See Files for all the papers file commands. papers filecheck is the deprecated form of these commands (it still works, with a warning).

docs.title: Listing and searching
docs.text: papers list is a powerful command, inspired by unix's find and grep. It lets you search your bibtex, output the result in a number of formats, or perform actions on the matched entries.

docs.title: Basic listing
docs.text:
Pretty listing by default (otherwise pass --plain for plain bibtex):

$> papers list
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

docs.title: Search with keywords
docs.text:
Search with any number of keywords:

$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level
... (short list)
$> papers list perrette scaling approach sea level --any
... (long list)
$> papers list --key perrette2013 --author perrette --year 2013 --title scaling approach sea level
... (precise list)

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags are the keywords field of the entries (comma-separated). papers tag lists them with the number of entries, adds and removes them:

$> papers tag perrette2013 --add sea-level projections
$> papers tag
sea-level (12)
projections (3)
$> papers tag perrette2013 --rm projections
$> papers tag --rename sea-level sea-level-rise     # in the whole library
$> papers list --tag sea-level projections
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1, sea-level | projections )

papers list ... --add-tag TAG... adds tags to the listed entries.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
papers list supports a number of special flags such as --duplicates, --review-required, --broken-file. --format chooses the output:

  • --format line (the default): one line per entry (also -l, -1, --one-liner);
  • --format bibtex: the entries as bibtex (also --plain);
  • --format key: the keys only, one per line (also -K, --key-only), to pipe into other commands (below).

--field FIELD... prints the key and the given fields of each entry (--no-key leaves the key out). -f is a deprecated alias of --field: in v4, -f is no longer --field (it means --force in other commands).

docs.title: Duplicates
docs.text:
papers list --duplicates lists the entries that are the same paper, by the rule of papers add (see Adding entries): the groups that papers check --duplicates would merge or ask about, and not the pairs recorded as distinct in .papers/distinct.json. With --invert, it lists the other entries.

With --fuzzy, it also lists the entries whose authors and title are similar (rapidfuzz token set ratio of at least --fuzzy-ratio, default 80). This is for looking only: papers never merges entries on this score.

With --by key, --by doi or --by title, it lists instead the entries that share that field: the same key (ignoring case), the same DOI, or the same title (ignoring case and punctuation), whether or not they are the same paper by the rule above (--by implies --duplicates).

--duplicates-key, --duplicates-doi and --duplicates-tit are deprecated forms of --duplicates --by key, --by doi and --by title; --similarity is deprecated and has no effect.

docs.title: Naming entries
docs.text:
The commands that act on entries take KEY arguments, where KEY is any of:

  • the key of the entry (case-insensitive), or a former key listed in its biblatex ids field (comma-separated);
  • a DOI: 10.1000/xyz, also written doi:10.1000/xyz or https://doi.org/10.1000/xyz (case-insensitive);
  • an arXiv identifier: 2101.01234, 2101.01234v2, arXiv:2101.01234, or of the old style hep-th/9901001; it matches the eprint field (when archivePrefix is arXiv or absent) and arXiv DOIs (10.48550/arXiv.<id>), whatever the version;
  • an ISBN, 10 or 13 digits, with hyphens or spaces (the ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 forms of a book are the same), matched against the isbn field.

A key cannot start with a digit, so an argument that starts with a digit is never a key. An identifier that matches no entry, or several entries (e.g. an ISBN shared by the chapters of a book), is an error, reported before anything changes.

docs.title: Piping
docs.text:
- reads the identifiers from the standard input, one per line (blank lines are ignored). papers list -K prints the keys of the listed entries, one per line:

papers list smith 2020 -K | papers file rename -
papers list --tag to-read -K | papers open -
papers list --no-file -K | papers check --fetch -
papers list --review-required -K | papers edit -

These commands take -: edit, rm, tag, open, check, and the papers file commands that act on entries (rename, check, and the --key option of detach and rm).

docs.title: Actions on the listed entries
docs.text:
papers list can also act on the entries it lists, as shortcuts of other commands:

  • -e/--edit: edit them in a text editor, as papers edit;
  • --delete: remove them, as papers rm (in a terminal, papers asks whether to delete their files too; --delete-files and --keep-files answer without asking, see Files);
  • --add-tag TAG...: add tags, as papers tag --add.

For instance, the duplicates can be edited by hand with (papers check --duplicates merges them, see Managing your library):

$> papers list --duplicates --edit

The file actions of papers list are deprecated, and print a warning that shows the new form; they will be removed in v4:

Deprecated New form papers list ... --rename (--copy) papers list ... -K \| papers file rename - (--keep-source) papers list ... --add-files FILE... papers file attach KEY FILE... papers list ... -o/--open papers list ... -K \| papers open - papers list ... --fetch papers list ... -K \| papers check --fetch --fetch-all --fix-doi --fix-key --format-name -

docs.title: Libraries and pools
docs.text:
A library is a bibtex file, a files directory and a configuration file (.papersconfig.json), as created by papers init (see Configuration). Each project usually has its own library.

A pool is a library that other libraries exchange entries with. Nothing in the pool marks it as a pool: a library acts as a pool when another library lists it in its pools setting. Any library can serve as a pool, and a pool can be used by several libraries. Separate pools (e.g. one per research field) are separate folders.

A library lists its pools as names or paths:

papers config pools default ../shared-with-bob

A name is looked up in the global configuration (papers pool add, below), so that the same project works on machines where the pool is in a different place. A path (it contains a /, or starts with . or ~) is relative to the library. Without global configuration, the name default is ~/Documents/papers, and a library created without --pool has "pools": ["default"]. A library never uses itself as a pool.

What a library does with its pools:

  • papers add looks in the pools first;
  • papers pull updates the entries of the library from the pools;
  • papers push adds entries of the library to its first pool, or updates them there;
  • papers status and papers pull --check tell whether a pool changed since the last pull.

Nothing is pulled or pushed automatically, except with the sync setting and in light libraries (below): an older project does not change because of work in a newer one.

A light library has no files of its own: its file links point to the files of its first pool (see Light libraries).

docs.title: Keys and identity
docs.text:
The key of an entry belongs to each library: it is what LaTeX documents cite. pull and push never change the key of the library they write to. A pool may name the same paper differently, and an entry new to a pool gets a key from the pool's key template.

A library entry and a pool entry are matched by the same rule as duplicates (see Same paper): same DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN (two books), or else the same authors and title. The pairs recorded as "not the same paper" (.papers/distinct.json) are merged both ways on pull and push.

docs.title: Origin copies
docs.text:
.papers/origin.bib, next to the bibtex of the library, records for each entry taken from a pool (by add, pull or push) the pool's version of the entry at that time, under the library's key, with the pool it came from (papers-pool), the key in the pool (papers-pool-key) and the time (papers-time). It also records the modification time of each pool's bibtex at the last pull. The file is part of the git backup of the library (see Git integration).

The origin copy is the third version of a three-way merge: comparing the library entry and the pool entry with it tells which side changed a field.

docs.title: add looks in the pools first
docs.text:
When the paper added is already in a pool, papers add takes the pool's entry, without querying crossref:

  • a PDF with the same content as a file of a pool entry, or whose DOI (from the PDF metadata, or a DOI of its text whose title in the pool appears in the text) is in a pool;
  • a DOI (papers add --doi DOI) that a pool entry has;
  • an entry of an added bibtex that is the same paper as a pool entry: the pool's fields are taken, the entry keeps its key, and its fields that the pool entry does not have are kept.

The entry gets the pool's files: in copy and move mode they are copied into the library's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the library's name template; a pool file is never moved. In link mode, and in a light library, the entry links to the pool's file. The origin copy is recorded. --no-pool skips the lookup.

With papers config sync push (default none), add also adds the entries new to the library to the first pool, as papers push would. Changes to existing entries are never pushed automatically.

docs.title: papers pull
docs.text:
papers pull [KEY...|-] [--on-duplicate MODE] [--check]

For each entry of the library (or the entries named), papers finds its pool entry (the pool of the origin copy first, then the pools in order) and merges it into the library entry, field by field:

Field changed since the origin copy Result in the pool only taken from the pool (+ in the dialogue) in the library only (e.g. a field adapted to a journal style) kept, without asking on both sides, to different values a conflict (!)

A field removed on one side keeps the other side's state: removed in the pool, it stays in the library; removed in the library, it does not come back. File links are merged: new files of the pool entry are copied into the library's files directory as the files setting says (linked in link mode and in light libraries). The key of the library entry never changes. After the merge, the origin copy is the pool's current version.

An entry without origin copy (added before the pool was used, or with --no-pool) is matched to the pools by the same-paper rule. Its differences with the pool entry are conflicts (there is no origin to tell which side changed), and the origin copy is recorded afterwards ("linked").

Conflicts are decided as for duplicates (see The dialogue), with --on-duplicate:

Mode Conflicts ask (default in a terminal) the dialogue: 1 keeps the library values, 2 takes the pool values, f goes field by field (also through the changes from the pool), e edits, s skips, q quits keep the library values are kept update the pool values are taken skip the entry is not changed, and its origin copy is not updated: it comes again next time error (default without a terminal) stop before saving anything

Fields changed in the pool only need no decision: they are taken in every mode.

papers pull --check only reports: whether each pool changed since the last pull (a modification time check), and the entries whose pool version changed since their origin copy, with the fields. papers status shows the first part too.

docs.title: papers push
docs.text:
papers push [KEY...|-] [--pool NAME|PATH] [--on-duplicate MODE]

The reverse of pull, into the first pool (or --pool):

  • an entry that is not in the pool is added to it, with a key from the pool's key template; its files are copied into the pool's files directory (a hard link when possible), named with the pool's name template;
  • an entry that is in the pool is merged three-way into the pool entry: fields changed in the library only are taken, fields changed in the pool only are kept, conflicts are decided with --on-duplicate (keep: the pool values, update: the library values). The pool key does not change.

The origin copies are updated. The default pool is created the first time something is pushed to it.

docs.title: papers export
docs.text:
papers export DIR [KEY...|-] [--files copy|link|none] [--pool]

writes the entries (all without KEY) as a new library in DIR, which must not exist or be empty: its bibtex, its files directory, and its configuration (with the name and key templates that the library sets). File links are relative to the new bibtex.

  • --files copy (default) copies the files into DIR/files (hard links when possible), named with the name template;
  • --files link links to the files where they are;
  • --files none leaves the file links out.

--pool also adds DIR to the pools of the library, and records the exported entries as origin copies: this turns a library into a pool. papers add DIR --recursive adds an exported library to another one.

docs.title: papers pool
docs.text:
The pool names of the global configuration:

papers pool add NAME PATH      # same as: papers config --global pools.NAME PATH
papers pool remove NAME
papers pool list               # or: papers pool

papers pool list shows the pools of the global configuration and those of the current library, with their paths and whether each changed since the last pull.

docs.title: Light libraries
docs.text:
A light library links to the files of its first pool instead of keeping its own. This saves the copies when many projects use the same papers. Being light changes what papers does with files:

  • add places new files in the first pool, named with the pool's name template (a name template set on the light library is not used), and so adds the entry to the pool too; papers file attach and papers file rename do the same with the files they place;
  • pull links to the pool's files instead of copying them;
  • rm --delete-files and file rm never delete a file of a pool (this holds in any library);
  • when a pool renames a file, the link breaks: it is repaired by looking the entry up in the pools, when the library is loaded (saved on the next write) and by papers file check --fix.

light is not a setting of papers config, because changing it changes the links and the files:

  • papers migrate --light replaces each file that the first pool has for the same paper, with the same content (checksum), by a link to the pool's file, and deletes the library's copy in its files directory. A file that is not in the pool is never deleted: the command lists those entries and asks to papers push them first. Then the library is light.
  • papers migrate --full copies (hard links when possible) the pool files that the library links to into its files directory, named with its name template, and relinks them. Then the library is not light any more.

papers init --light creates a light library.

Deleting a file in a pool breaks the links of the light libraries that use it: it shows up as a broken link there (papers file check). The pool keeps no list of the libraries that depend on it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A shared pool in ~/Documents/papers, and two projects:

papers init ~/Documents/papers            # the default pool
mkdir -p ~/projects/sealevel ~/projects/tides
cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers init                               # pools: default
papers add ~/Downloads/esd-4-11-2013.pdf  # fetched from crossref, files/...
papers push                               # now also in ~/Documents/papers

cd ~/projects/tides
papers init
papers add --doi 10.5194/esd-4-11-2013    # taken from the pool: no query, the file is copied

Later, the entry is completed in the pool (e.g. its pages), and adapted in tides (a journal abbreviation):

cd ~/projects/tides
papers status                  # pools: ... (changed since last pull)
papers pull --check            # perrette_landerer2013: changed in pool default: pages
papers pull                    # pages taken; the journal abbreviation is kept

A project shared with a colleague: export it as its own library, used as a second pool by both:

cd ~/projects/sealevel
papers export ../shared-with-bob --pool   # pools: default ../shared-with-bob
papers push --pool ../shared-with-bob     # later changes

To save disk space in tides, make it light once its files are in the pool:

papers push
papers migrate --light

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This tool's interface is built like git, with a main command papers and a range of subcommands. This page walks through the most common first steps.

docs.title: Extract PDF metadata and add to library
docs.text:
Start with a PDF of your choice (modern enough to have a DOI, e.g. anything from the Copernicus publications). For the sake of the example, one of mine: https://www.earth-syst-dynam.net/4/11/2013/esd-4-11-2013.pdf

Extract the PDF metadata (DOI-based if available, otherwise crossref, or google scholar if so specified):

$> papers extract esd-4-11-2013.pdf
@article{Perrette_2013,
doi = {10.5194/esd-4-11-2013},
url = {https://doi.org/10.5194%2Fesd-4-11-2013},
year = 2013,
month = {jan},
publisher = {Copernicus {GmbH}},
volume = {4},
number = {1},
pages = {11--29},
author = {M. Perrette and F. Landerer and R. Riva and K. Frieler and M. Meinshausen},
title = {A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and its uncertainties},
journal = {Earth System Dynamics}
}

Add the PDF to your papers.bib library, and rename a copy of it in a files directory files:

$> papers add esd-4-11-2013.pdf --copy --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files --info
INFO:papers:found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:new entry: perrette_landerer2013
INFO:papers:ln /home/perrette/playground/papers/esd-4-11-2013.pdf files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach-to-project-regional-sea-level-rise-and-its-uncertainties.pdf
INFO:papers:renamed file(s): 1

(the --info argument asks for the above output information to be printed out to the terminal)

--copy keeps the original PDF where it is (a hard link when possible); without it the PDF is moved into the files directory, and with --link it is left where it is and the entry links to it there. The files setting of a library sets the default (see Files).

See Adding entries for the full range of ways to add entries, and Renaming files and keys for how to specify file naming patterns.

docs.title: List entries
docs.text:
Pretty listing by default (otherwise pass --plain for plain bibtex):

$> papers list
Perrette2013: A scaling approach to project regional sea level rise and it... (doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013, file:1)

See Listing and searching for the full power of papers list.

docs.title: Make settings persistent
docs.text:
In the common case where the bibtex, files directory and naming formats do not change, create a library so that you don't need to pass them every time:

papers init --bibtex papers.bib --filesdir files

Commands run in that directory (or below) then act on this library. See Configuration for details.

Tip

Consult the inline help (papers --help, papers <command> --help) for more detailed documentation of every option.

docs.title: Entries with several files
docs.text:
The first file of an entry (the PDF) is named after the name template, and any other file (attachments, e.g. supplementary material added with --attach or papers file attach) is placed next to it, under the same name followed by -- and the file's original name:

files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach.pdf
files/perrette_et_al_2013_a-scaling-approach--esd-4-11-2013-supplement.pdf

The label after -- is kept when the entry is renamed again (e.g. after its title or year was fixed), so only the part before -- changes. If two attachments have the same original name, the second one gets a -2 suffix.

Versions before 2.19 placed the files of an entry with several files in a folder named after the entry, with a hidden copy of the entry (files/<name>/.<name>.bib). Such folders keep working as they are: their files are linked from the bibtex, and nothing is moved until the entry is renamed. Renaming (papers file rename) moves the files out of the folder into the layout above, and removes the folder if nothing but the hidden bibtex is left in it (a folder with other files is kept, and the files left in it are reported).

docs.title: Renaming the files of existing entries
docs.text:
papers add places new files in the files directory under their template name (unless the files setting is link, see Files). To rename the files of entries already in the library, e.g. after changing the name template or fixing an entry's title:

papers file rename                      # all entries
papers file rename perrette2013         # some entries
papers list --year 2013 -K | papers file rename -

Each file is moved into the files directory under its new name; --keep-source keeps the original too (a hard link when possible). A file that belongs to another library is copied, not moved. The deprecated papers filecheck --rename and papers list ... --rename run this command.

docs.title: Control fields when renaming files
docs.text:
$> papers add --move --info --name-template "{AuthorX}{year}-{Title}" --name-title-sep '' --name-author-sep '' esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:found doi:10.5194/esd-4-11-2013
INFO:papers:new entry: perrette2013scaling
INFO:papers:create directory: files/2013
INFO:papers:mv /home/perrette/playground/papers/esd-4-11-2013.pdf files/PerretteEtAl2013-AScalingApproachToProjectRegionalSeaLevelRiseAndItsUncertainties.pdf
INFO:papers:renamed file(s): 1

where --name-template is a python template (formatted via the .format() method) with valid fields being any field available in the bibtex. Fields not in the bibtex will remain untouched.

To rename esd-4-11-2013.pdf as perrette_2013.pdf, the template should be --name-template {author}_{year} --name-author-num 1. If that happens to be the entry ID, ID also works.

To rename esd-4-11-2013.pdf as 2013/Perrette2013-AScalingApproachToProjectRegionalSeaLevelRiseAndItsUncertainties.pdf, name-template should be --name-template {year}/{Author}{year}-{Title} --name-title-sep '' (note the case).

docs.title: Case-sensitive fields
docs.text:
Entries are case-sensitive, and a few more fields are added, so that:

  • author generates perrette
  • Author generates Perrette
  • AUTHOR generates PERRETTE
  • authorX generates perrette, perrette_and_landerer or perrette_et_al depending on the number of authors
  • AuthorX same as authorX but capitalized

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
The modifiers are:

  • --name-title-sep: separator for title words
  • --name-title-length: max title length
  • --name-title-word-size: min size to be considered a word
  • --name-title-word-num: max number of title words

and similarly:

  • --name-author-sep: separator for authors
  • --name-author-num: number of authors (not relevant for {authorX})

and for entries without author, year or title:

  • --name-unknown-template: the template used instead (default: unknown_{doi_or_id} for file names, {doi_} for keys)
  • --name-unknown-strict: use it only when author, year and title are all missing

The same template and modifiers system applies to the bibtex key generation by replacing the prefix --name- with --key-, e.g. --key-template.

In the common case where the bibtex (--bibtex), files directory (--filesdir), and name and key formats (e.g. --name-template) do not change, it is convenient to store them in a library configuration (papers init, papers config name.template ...).

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Did a papers add and are unhappy with the result?

papers undo

will revert to the previous version. Without git-tracking, repeating it only jumps back and forth between the latest and before-latest version.

With git-tracking (the default for fresh installs), papers undo and papers redo step through the whole history of the library (-n N steps at once). History is append-only: undo and redo record restore commits in the backup repository instead of rewriting it, so no state is ever lost. In particular, making a new change while undone starts a new line of history on top, and the states that were still redoable remain reachable with further papers undo or with papers restore --ref COMMIT (use papers git log to find COMMIT). papers restore without --ref restores the last version of the backup. papers restore-backup is the deprecated name of papers restore.

See Git integration for how to enable git-tracking.
